checks.location: Theorem2: arbitrary polynomial-filter expressivity and AppendixA.1 construction; Section4.2 Theorem2 and AppendixA.1 complete proof
checks.claim: Theorem2: arbitrary polynomial-filter expressivity and AppendixA.1 construction; Section4.2 Theorem2 and AppendixA.1 complete proof
checks.explanation: ReLU makes every final hidden coordinate nonnegative, whereas an arbitrary polynomial filter can produce a negative output from positive input. The proof drops ReLU after checking the input sign, but its learned scalar multipliers can still make a preactivation negative.
checks.demonstration:
Take the graph with one vertex and its self-loop. Its normalized propagation matrix is $\widetilde P=[1]$ and its Laplacian is $\widetilde L=[0]$. Let $x=1$ and choose the degree-$1$ filter $p(\lambda)=\lambda-1$. The claimed output is
$$p(\widetilde L)x=-1.$$
Equation (5), however, makes every final hidden coordinate at least zero for every choice of weights. Consequently, the displayed equality fails already with one layer.

The proof has the same obstruction. With $\alpha=\tfrac12$, positive input and hidden state equal to $1$, and effective scalar weight $\gamma=-1$, the preactivation is $-1$, whereas ReLU returns $0$. Nonnegative input therefore does not justify replacing the layer by its linear preactivation. The proof also acknowledges zero denominators in its coefficient-ratio construction and substitutes approximation, which does not establish the stated exact equality.
checks.repair:
State the result for a modified output that takes a signed linear combination of the input and all intermediate layer states, rather than identify the polynomial with the final ReLU state. This gives an exact constructive theorem while keeping the graph-convolution layers in Equation (5).

For $x\geq0$, set each effective weight to the identity and fix $0<\alpha<1$. Since $\widetilde P$ is entrywise nonnegative, all preactivations remain nonnegative and
$$h^{(0)}=x,\qquad h^{(\ell+1)}=(1-\alpha)\widetilde P h^{(\ell)}+\alpha x=q_{\ell+1}(\widetilde P)x,$$
where $q_0(z)=1$ and $q_{\ell+1}(z)=(1-\alpha)zq_\ell(z)+\alpha$. Each $q_\ell$ has degree $\ell$ and nonzero leading coefficient $(1-\alpha)^\ell$. Therefore $q_0,\ldots,q_K$ form a basis for polynomials of degree at most $K$. For any desired filter $p(\widetilde L)=r(\widetilde P)$, solve the triangular polynomial system $r=\sum_{\ell=0}^K c_\ell q_\ell$ and use the readout $\sum_{\ell=0}^K c_\ell h^{(\ell)}$. The coefficients $c_\ell$ may be signed; no denominator depends on a target coefficient, so zeros are allowed. For arbitrary signed $x$, propagate the two nonnegative channels $x_+=\max(x,0)$ and $x_-=\max(-x,0)$ and subtract their readouts.

This is a proved correction with an explicit layerwise readout. Merely pointing to the implementation's existing dense layer on the final state would not establish the same result.
checks.scope: The counterexample concerns exact equality between a polynomial-filter output and the final ReLU features. The original implementation already places a dense output layer after those features; that implementation choice is not a later correction. The repaired theorem uses a signed readout of $h^{(0)},\ldots,h^{(K)}$, whereas the released classifier reads only $h^{(K)}$.
checks.verificationNote: The original hidden-feature equality is false; a signed readout of every layer gives a complete exact polynomial construction.
checks.title: The final ReLU features cannot equal arbitrary signed polynomial filters
checks.contextBefore: GCNII combines graph propagation with an initial-feature residual and a learned weight matrix, then applies ReLU. Appendix A.1 specializes the effective weight matrix to a learned scalar $\gamma_\ell$ times the identity.
checks.claimContext: Theorem 2 claims that a $K$-layer GCNII expresses every order-$K$ polynomial graph filter with arbitrary coefficients. Section 4.2 identifies that filtered signal with the final features $h^{(K)}$, while Equation (5) applies ReLU at every graph-convolution layer.
checks.whyItMatters: The expressivity theorem promises every polynomial filter, including signed responses and zero coefficients. The final ReLU state cannot satisfy that promise. The explicit readout of all layer states gives a corrected output for which the polynomial-basis argument is valid.

checks.claim: d_TV(P_eff, P_u) <= (1-alpha)(1-rho_q pi_q) + alpha d_TV(P_l, P_u), where P_u and the pseudo-labeled distribution are distributions over (S, B) sharing the S-marginal, rho_q is event-level coverage and pi_q is box-level precision.
checks.explanation: Box-level precision and true-event coverage do not give the probability that a complete annotation set is correct. A detector can cover every true event while adding a false box to every spectrogram. Every full annotation is then different from the target, even though coverage is one and some predicted boxes are exactly correct.
checks.demonstration:
Use one fixed spectrogram with a true annotation set $B=\{b\}$. Let the pseudo annotation be $\widetilde B=\{b,b'\}$, where the added box $b'$ is disjoint from the true box. The true box is predicted exactly, so coverage is $\rho_q=1$. One of the two predicted boxes is correct, giving precision $\pi_q=1/2$.

The complete annotation laws are different point masses. Take $P_\ell=P_u$ and $\alpha=1/2$. The effective training law assigns mass $1/2$ to each annotation, so

$$d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P_{\mathrm{eff}},P_u)=\frac12.$$

The proposed bound instead gives $(1-\alpha)(1-\rho_q\pi_q)=1/4$. The input marginal is identical, and the matched box is exact, so the contradiction does not depend on any ambiguity about localization tolerance. With more exactly predicted true boxes and one extra false box, precision can be arbitrarily close to one while every full annotation still differs.
checks.repair:
Use an error probability defined on complete annotations. Under a shared-input coupling, let $\varepsilon=\Pr(\widetilde B\ne B)$. The coupling inequality and convexity give

$$d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P_{\mathrm{eff}},P_u)\le(1-\alpha)\varepsilon+\alpha d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P_\ell,P_u).$$

This is valid, but $\varepsilon$ is not supplied by the reported IoU precision and coverage. To regard small localization shifts as small errors, use a geometric distance on annotations and derive a bound for that distance. Even with exact pseudo labels, fixed positive anchoring weight and a different source distribution need not converge to the target distribution.
checks.scope: The proposition’s total-variation bound is false under its stated annotation model. The complete-annotation coupling repair uses a different error quantity, so it does not restore the original precision–coverage guarantee.
checks.title: Detection precision and coverage do not bound joint annotation total variation
checks.claimContext: Proposition 5 compares distributions of complete spectrogram–annotation pairs $(S,B)$, with $B$ a set of time–frequency boxes. It bounds their total variation using box precision $\pi_q$ and true-event coverage $\rho_q$, where a detection counts as matched at intersection-over-union at least $1/2$. The effective training law is $P_{\mathrm{eff}}=(1-\alpha)\widehat P_u+\alpha P_\ell$.
checks.whyItMatters: Event-level detection scores do not determine how often an entire spectrogram has the correct annotation set. A distributional guarantee must use an error quantity defined on the same space as the probability distance.

Fix one input channel \(i\), one output channel \(o\), and \(C\ge k\). For any target matrix \(M\in\mathbb R^{k\times k}\), set
\[W_t[m,i,a]=\mathbf1\{m=a\},\qquad W_f[o,m,b]=M[m,b]\quad(1\le m\le k),\]
and set unused intermediate contributions to zero. Then
\[K_{o,i}[a,b]=\sum_{m=1}^kM[m,b]\mathbf1\{m=a\}=M[a,b].\]
In particular, \(k=C=3\) and \(M=I_3\) give rank three, so the effective kernel is nonseparable. Padding unused channels preserves the example when the model has more channels. Keep the parameter count, receptive-field calculation and exact per-pair rank bound, but remove the unconditional nonseparability exclusion. A useful joint restriction follows by grouping indices: define

checks.contextBefore:
We use the fine-grained descriptions generated through HolisticCap and encode visual and textual features in the CLIP embedding space.
We treat each multimodal embedding (concatenation of the two modalities) as a query and use a simple nearest neighbour search to create bags of highly similar images.
Algorithm 1 provides details on the bag creation process, especially for creating bags of variable size.
Having bags of varying size facilitates SR evaluation at multiple levels of difficulty as increasing the bag size limits the number visual concepts that can be used to uniquely describe each image.
This is different from previous works that typically use image pairs (Jhamtani & Berg-Kirkpatrick, 2018, Park et al., 2019, Tong et al., 2024b) or random distractors (Dessì et al., 2023) to evaluate captioners.
